message.content:
**Q1.** Keep fixed λ = 1. Nested CV loses 8.7 pp (SD 5.5 on 9 blocks; not past 1.96 SD) and 9.4 pp in 1970s–80s origins because early windows select λ = 30–100 where pre-1966 inner skill is negative. Eleven designs span only +18.0 to +23.4, all below fixed +27.05. Nine to thirteen episode blocks cannot identify λ; inner folds over-penalise the full-window refit. Today’s CV λ = 3 moves P(+1.11) only 15.1 → 15.8, inside the band. Post hoc is acceptable: the preregistered ablation already predicted nested ∈ [+17, +25] and it held; we are not relaxing a failed threshold, we are refusing a selector that lost. Headline from 2027 is fixed-λ walk-forward. Nested and oracle-free (+20.4) print in the same sentence, labelled non-operational.

**Q2.** Amend §4. No selector runs. Inner CV picked F5 in 100% of origins from 2000 and every non-degenerate rule lost 9–10 pp versus nested curve, almost all of it in the 2022–24 false alarm (−11.0 pp). F5’s inner advantage is 75.7% one block (6 rows, 1947Q2–1948Q3); without it the advantage clears 4.42 pp in 0% of origins. Pearson(inner, realised) = −0.16. Curve-only stays operational by council lock, not by search. Gate: print Δ against the gate’s own MDE (21.06 pp) only. |Δ| > own MDE → next council agenda, still no switch. Drop 4.42 as an action trigger; it is the frequency test’s MDE and will agenda noise (E3 gate swings −3.9 to −31 pp by start date alone).

**Q3.** Quarterly fit. Full monthly +29.24 (591) versus quarterly +27.05 (198) is +2.19 pp against block-MDE 2.99. The code reading fails by 0.02 pp on one phase; that is a documented bug, not a result. The two series use different origins and different pooled base rates; 591 overlapping windows are not 591 observations. Live input is already a trailing month, so §2’s timeliness claim is met without a monthly fit. Counterfactual P is 14.4 versus 14.9. Both readings are known, so the status quo wins. Do not retune the gate so the literal reading “passes.”

**Q4.** Keep 1947Q2. On the 158 common origins skill is +20.5 / +21.4 / +21.9 — flat. The full-sample gaps are composition (pre-1960 positives 36.6% versus 14.6% after), not a better DGP. Moving the start cuts live P from 14.9 to 12.4 or 10.4, and we have seen that. Verdict word is unchanged at every start. Print the three-start line every release. F5’s collapse at 1953Q2 (−0.73) and 1960Q1 (+3.71) is a benchmark warning, not a reason to shorten the curve sample.

**Q5.** Nothing operational. “Five incumbents pass” is an artefact of the asymmetric bar. Incumbent-as-challenger and both elimination orders end at curve-only; the other symmetry demotes nobody. Curve+cape +2.64 pp fails pre-1990 (−0.34), sits below MDE 4.42, and far below the gate’s own MDE. Document that. Any future search, if ever mandated, uses one symmetric bar written in the sealed spec before any run. Do not treat +2.64 as a near-miss that justifies a cape spec.

**Q6.** Reject the content trigger. Keep September + hash. Historical mean |ΔP| is 0.13 pp, max 1.05, on 53 of 588 months; the projected non-September case is 0.37 pp for 9 months. That is inside a band several percentage points wide. Eighteen extra refits in 49 years buy weight-path churn to remove a remainder that is smaller than the 18-month floor already imposed. The counterfactual was seen. A mechanical trigger whose only demonstrated effect is 0.13 pp is not worth a protocol fork.

**Q7.** Do not amend the key. It was pushed before row 4; E5 is exactly the information that must not rewrite the scoreboard. Publish a supplement with three censoring variants side by side: real-time +24.41 (561 rows), no USREC-vintage assumption +28.95, oracle +33.28. State in the same sentence as any skill claim: cluster-t reaches 80% power at about 150 calendar years (about 18 if the 2020–24 block is dropped from the pool); 3 complete cycle blocks arrive within 20 years with probability 0.25; naive iid and the key’s 4.4-block bootstrap reject a true null 36–53% of the time at 5–20 years. Also state that the logged base rate averages 22.8% against a realised onset rate of 15.3%, so key skill is not a pooled-ex-post skill (that figure is +21.2%). The ledger is an honesty log, not a test.

**Q8.** Close. Onset values have been seen (high before 1990 and 2001, low before 1980, 2008, 2020). That spends the researcher degrees of freedom a sealed test would need. EBP can revise monthly; Baa cannot be redistributed; about 3 pre-1990 EBP onsets against MDE ≈ 4.4 pp. “Defer until 12 clean snapshots” is a back door onto the same inspected history. Reopening requires a new economic rationale, a council mandate, and a sealed spec that does not use the already-seen onset pattern. Practically that means closed.

**Q9.** Peak-only, locked before the first audit run. The label is onset; the binding lag is peak announcement to peak date. Formula: L_R = max(18, maximum peak-announcement lag in months). Trough announcements (20–21 in 1991 and 2001) do not determine onset labels and must not enter the max. Including them now would lift L_R to 21 and change eligible origins after that effect is known. This is a definition fixed before the audit, not a threshold relaxed after a score.

**Q10.** Ratify all four, two with conditions. (2) and (3) are a restoration of R3 and a line already in the preregistered key — ratify as written. (1) ratify the trailing-month DGS10−DTB3 as the live input only if every ledger row permanently carries P on the historical monthly GS10−TB3MS beside it; the walk-forward remains on the monthly series. (4) ratify live censoring only if the rule is byte-identical to the scoring key’s open-episode rule and written into the protocol before the 2027 refit. E5 shows the censoring definition moves replay skill by 4.5 pp; an informal live rule is not acceptable.

**Claude.** D1 keep, but the operational headline is fixed-λ only; the pair is a disclosure, not a menu. D2 amend: delete the 4.42 agenda tier. D3 keep. D4 keep. D5 keep, plus an explicit bar on citing curve+cape +2.64 as a sealed-test candidate. D6 strike. D7 keep, and add the 22.8-versus-15.3 base-rate gap and the 36–53% false-rejection rates to the public sentence, not the supplement. D8 strike; close, do not defer. D9 keep. D10 amend as in Q10.

**Biggest risk.** Status-quo lock after seeing the numbers. Fixed λ, 1947Q2, quarterly fit, and no content trigger all preserve the higher skill headline and a P near 15% rather than 10%. A hostile reading is that the council chose the specification that keeps the verdict “not distinguishable” and the backtest at +27%. The quantitative defence holds — alternatives lose preregistered comparisons or move P inside a band that already contains the base rate — but it fails in public if +27% leads and the 150-year power result sits in a supplement. The power clause has to occupy the same sentence as the headline or the backtest becomes the product’s claimed accuracy, which the ledger cannot check.
message.reasoning:
I am Grok 4.7. I will draft my independent proposal for the council.

I am weighing the evidence for Q1. Fixed λ=1 outperforms nested cross-validation by roughly 8.7 percentage points. Nested CV loses about 9.4 points in the 1970s and 1980s because its inner folds select λ values of 30–100 during early windows where the skill curve was negative before 1966.

The bootstrap test is not statistically significant. The 9–13 episode blocks are too small for reliable inner-fold λ selection. I largely agree with Claude D1: keep λ=1 as a fixed protocol constant and print both figures. The point estimate loss of 8.7 percentage points is large enough to matter even if the test is not formally significant.

The fixed-λ walk-forward remains the headline figure. Nested and oracle-free results will be printed beside it to avoid letting the worse number become the headline.

For Q2, nested selection picks F5 in every origin from 2000 onward. That choice costs 9–10 percentage points versus the nested curve. F5’s inner-CV edge of 72–76% is drawn from a single six-row block covering 1947–1948.

The correlation between inner-CV advantage and realized advantage is only -0.16. The selector is anti-skilled.

I agree with the amendment to §4: no selector, curve-only locked by council decision.

For the gate, using the frequency test’s 4.42 percentage point threshold is flawed. F5’s start-sensitivity swings exceed 20 points, so a borrowed threshold would fire on noise. Claude’s two-tier logic is reasonable but still relies on that borrowed number. E3 shows F5 gate differences of -3.89, -31, and -18 depending on origin.

The F5 benchmark gate should not use the 4.42 percentage point threshold as an action trigger at all. The council agenda should only open when the gate’s own MDE is exceeded or a new economic rationale appears. Claude’s borrowed threshold would generate false council items.

For Q3, quarterly data scores +27.05 and full monthly data scores +29.24. The literal reading passes, but the code reading fails by 0.02 percentage points on one thinning phase. The difference between full and quarterly monthly is +2.19 versus an MDE of 2.99 for v5.0.1. The confidence interval excludes zero yet does not clear the MDE.

The 591 monthly windows are not independent, and the live input is already monthly. The counterfactual gap between monthly and quarterly is only 0.5 percentage points, which is economically negligible.

The +2 percentage point edge does not clear the block-level MDE, so switching to monthly would amount to choosing after seeing the result. I will keep the status quo of quarterly data. The 0.02 percentage point code failure is a bug to document, not a reason to change the protocol or retrospectively adjust the gate.

Moving the universe start backward lowers P by 2.5 to 4.5 percentage points. That is exactly the kind of post-hoc lowering the rules forbid. Walk-forward on common origins is flat at roughly 20.5, 21.4, and 21.9 percentage points. The full-sample differences are composition effects across different origin sets and base rates, not evidence of a better sample. Pre-1960 positives are 36.6 percent versus 14.6 percent, but that is a regime shift already captured by the protocol sample and Shiller LTR splice. F5 is wildly start-sensitive; curve-only is not evaluated on common origins. I will keep 1947Q2 as the fixed start, print the sensitivity analysis, and agree with Claude D4.

The post-hoc problem is decisive: we already know the P effect.

For Q5, the asymmetric demotion rule kept incumbents; symmetric "incumbent as challenger" ends at curve-only; alternative symmetry demotes nobody. Outcome depends on which symmetry. Cape plus four-point-one-one and two-point-three-seven only holds in five of eight folds. Neutral log-likelihood gives curve plus cape plus two-point-six-four percentage points, fails pre-1990, and sits below the MDE. Nothing operational comes from this. Document the asymmetry. Future search will use one symmetric bar sealed before the run. Feature search is closed. Do not reopen for cape.

I agree with D5 but will strengthen it. The +2.64 percentage point curve-plus-cape result is below the MDE and fails G2, G3, and G5. It must not be cited as a near-miss that justifies a sealed cape test.

For Q6, eighteen extra refits in forty-nine years produced mean |ΔP| of 0.13 percentage points and a maximum of 1.05. The delay ranges from zero to nine months depending on the onset month. This is purely mechanical. The current rule’s delay is an artifact of announcement timing rather than economics. Adopting it does not change the current prediction before the 2027 refit. The only benefit is removing a timing lottery.

I disagree with Claude on the content trigger. Eighteen extra refits add complexity and risk weight-path dependence and frozen-weight discrepancies. The mean absolute difference of 0.13 percentage points is noise within a roughly ten-point estimation band. A nine-month delay yields only 0.37 percentage points. The eighteen-month floor already dominates timing. This trigger solves a negligible problem. I will reject or amend D6. September plus hash remains.

Reconsidering the content trigger: omitting a known onset from the fit for nine months is a real protocol defect, not merely a cosmetic P adjustment. The isolated effect is roughly 0.37 to 0.44 percentage points. The 1980–81 censoring issue in E5 is far larger. The trigger corrects when matured positives enter the fit, not open episodes; historically it delays entry by about eighty-five origin-months.

The content trigger would slightly flatten the curve coefficient by excluding recent onsets from the training sample. Those omitted months are often inside the recession and censored from scoring anyway. The lag in learning is small and within the estimation band.

I will reject the content trigger. The effect is too small to justify eighteen extra refits, and the rule was chosen after seeing the counterfactual. September plus hash already catches hash changes, and the eighteen-month floor is the economically relevant lag.

For Q7, I will not amend the preregistered ledger key.

E5 confirms the ledger is not a test. Real-time censoring drops P by 83 open-episode months, including the 1980–81 run-up. The logged base rate of 22.8 percent versus the realized 15.3 percent makes the reference too generous. Power is only 80 percent at roughly 150 calendar years; cluster-t is 1.37 and naive tests reject the null 36 to 53 percent of the time. The public statement must be harsh: the ledger is not a test.

The key’s minimum of three cycle blocks has only a 25 percent chance of being reached in twenty years. Early ledger skill must not be treated as confirmation or disconfirmation. The +20.4 percent reference stays unchanged because it is preregistered; the supplement should publish all three censoring variants and flag that the logged base rate is upward-biased versus the realized onset rate, so the key’s skill is not directly comparable to a pooled-ex-post benchmark without adjustment. Claude D7 is mostly correct.

I will amend the public statement for Q7 to explicitly flag that the logged-base-rate rule inflates apparent skill versus a realized-rate benchmark, and that the key’s block-bootstrap tests are anti-conservative with 36–53 percent false rejection. The scoreboard itself must not be changed; only these findings should be disclosed.

For Q8, I will close the EBP/Baa test rather than defer it. Onset values were already observed before the 1990, 2001, 1980, 2008, and 2020 thresholds, so contamination is fatal for a preregistered test.

The EBP/Baa test is closed. Only about three of eight onsets predate 1990, so the sample is too small for a meaningful test. A sealed future test would be theater because the feature search is already complete. Deferral until twelve snapshots show no revision still leaves the observed onset pattern as a hypothesis tested on the same history.

For Q9, L_R is the annual audit of announcement lag for the eighteen-month floor. The current code measures peak-to-peak lags and yields eighteen. Including trough-to-peak lags would raise L_R to twenty-one and alter eligible origins. The label remains onset.

Peak-only lag is correct because the eighteen-month floor is justified by NBER announcement timing for the onset label. Trough announcements do not alter onsets. Locking L_R at eighteen before the audit begins is proper definition of the metric, not post-hoc threshold relaxation.

The L_R formula is now explicit: it equals the maximum of the eighteen-month floor and the peak-announcement lag, with trough announcements excluded from that maximum. This definition must be locked before the first audit run.

For Q10, the ratification review has begun. The first F29 change noted is the live curve shift from the latest published monthly GS10−TB3MS to the trailing month of daily DGS10−DTB3.

The remaining three F29 changes are already in operation. Swarm tripwires moved out of the ignition column, restoring R3. The log-day rule is the first weekday from the tenth plus three days. Live censoring applies to readings inside an announced recession.

Ratifying these after the fact is awkward but preferable to undocumented drift. The daily-trailing-month input is a real specification break because the model was historically fit and scored on monthly GS10−TB3MS.

The daily-trailing-month input is a live operational change, but the walk-forward must continue on the historical monthly series. The discrepancy between the two inputs must be published every row from row 4 onward; this dual-reporting requirement should be made permanent rather than optional.

Restoring R3 is a restoration of an earlier decision, not a new choice, so it should be ratified. The log-day rule is already documented in the preregistered key and should be ratified as documentation. Live censoring inside an announced recession is consistent with the label definition, so it should also be ratified.

The live curve must match the scoring key exactly so replay and live do not diverge. The four F29 changes are now fully ratified, with conditions on the daily-trailing-month input and live censoring.

Claude’s draft is kept for D1 but amended: the headline must remain a fixed-λ operational skill, not a co-equal pair that lets readers pick. For D2, the 4.42 agenda trigger should be dropped; prints should gate on Δ versus own MDE only.

D3 through D9 are kept as written. D5 should add a warning that curve-plus-cape +2.64 is not a candidate for a sealed test. D6 is struck; only the September plus hash trigger remains. The single biggest risk in my own proposal is now being identified.

The single biggest risk is the content trigger. A known positive can sit out of the fit for up to nine months, and a steep next recession curve could make that omission matter more than the historical 0.37 percentage point. Keeping λ fixed at one and locking the 1947Q2 baseline also risks looking like P-management to outsiders, even though the defense is legitimate.

The real risk is post-hoc status-quo bias. Rejecting every change that would lower headline skill or P makes the council look like it locked the specification that maximizes reported performance. The defense is quantitative: alternatives fail preregistered comparisons, move P into a band already containing the base rate, and thresholds are not being relaxed.

The single biggest risk is reputational capture by the status quo. The headline skill of +27 percent is an in-sample-of-the-protocol number that E5 shows the live ledger cannot confirm for 150 years. Making this unconfirmable backtest the permanent headline would let the public treat a backtest as the product’s accuracy.
